author.name: Multiple drafters and assemblies
author.years: Late eighteenth century, with later amendments
author.occupation: Multiple drafters, assemblies and political actors
author.biography: The Declaration, Constitution and amendments emerged from different assemblies, writers and political struggles. Their authorship is collective, contested and unfinished in a way no single portrait can capture. Their makers declared principles of freedom while living within systems that denied it to many others. Later amendments changed who could claim those promises and what protection they offered. Reading the documents together means encountering both the ambition of a founding and the work of revising it.

hook.text: What do you do when a country fails to live by its own promises?

paragraphs: A declaration gives reasons for political separation. A constitution distributes authority. Amendments place protections and new commitments into the structure. Read together, the founding documents show a political order trying to state what it is for and how it is meant to work.

The statements are powerful partly because they can be used against the failures of the people who first endorsed them. Claims about equality and liberty existed beside slavery and exclusion. Later struggles would ask whether the promises belonged to everyone or only to those initially able to claim them.
Pay attention to the different jobs the documents perform. An ideal does not by itself create an institution, and an institution can distribute power without settling every question of justice.
What should loyalty to a country's founding commitments require when those commitments become the strongest reason to demand that the country change?

orientation.text: Read each document with its date and purpose in view. The collection moves from the Declaration to the Constitution, the Bill of Rights and later amendments; each does a different kind of political work.
